mcqs.question: A 10-million-row table has an `is_deleted` boolean column. Why is it a poor standalone index candidate?
options: With only 2 distinct values, a filter on it matches roughly half the table — low selectivity means the planner will likely prefer a full scan anyway
Booleans cannot be indexed by any relational database
Boolean indexes require twice as much disk space as integer indexes
It would need to be rebuilt every time the value changes
mcqs.explanation: Low cardinality means low selectivity — an equality filter matches a large fraction of rows, which usually makes a full scan cheaper than random index lookups. Booleans can absolutely be indexed, don't need double the space, and don't require special rebuild handling beyond normal index maintenance.

mcqs.question: Why does using a randomly-ordered UUID as a primary key hurt performance more on MySQL InnoDB than on Postgres?
options: UUIDs are not supported as primary keys in InnoDB

InnoDB clusters the table physically by primary key, so a random UUID scatters row insertion order across the whole table — Postgres's heap is already unordered, so this cost doesn't apply the same way
Postgres compresses UUIDs automatically while InnoDB does not
InnoDB requires primary keys to be sequential integers only
mcqs.explanation: Because InnoDB's clustered index IS the table's physical layout, a random primary key scatters inserts across pages, unlike Postgres where the heap is unordered by default regardless of key choice. UUIDs are supported in InnoDB, there's no such automatic compression difference, and InnoDB doesn't require sequential keys, just performs better with them.

mcqs.question: A table has a standard index on `email`, but `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com'` still does a full scan. Why?
options: The query has a syntax error that silently disables index usage
Functions can never be used in a WHERE clause with an indexed column
The index only stores raw `email` values in sorted order; `LOWER(email)` computes a different value per row that doesn't match any position in that tree
The `email` column must be re-indexed after every query
mcqs.explanation: A B+Tree index is built on the stored, unmodified value; wrapping the column in a function produces a different value at query time that has no defined position in that tree, so the index can't be used. There's no syntax error, functions can be used in WHERE clauses generally, and no per-query reindexing is required.

mcqs.question: Why would `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'` be smaller and cheaper than a full index on `created_at`?
options: Partial indexes use a more compact binary format automatically
Partial indexes don't require any disk space at all
It indexes all rows but compresses non-matching ones
It only indexes rows matching the WHERE condition, so if just 2% of rows are pending, the index is roughly 2% the size and cheaper to maintain on writes to other rows
mcqs.explanation: A partial index only contains entries for rows matching its WHERE clause, so its size scales with the matching subset, not the whole table — and writes to non-matching rows don't touch it at all. There's no special compact format, it does use real disk space, and it doesn't index all rows.

mcqs.question: On a multi-tenant table, you're building a composite index on `tenant_id` and `status` (5 possible values), both filtered with equality. Which column should lead the index?
options: `status`, because it should always come after `tenant_id` alphabetically
`tenant_id`, because it narrows the search to one tenant's rows immediately, a much smaller slice than one-fifth of the entire table
It doesn't matter which comes first for equality-only composite indexes
`status`, because leading with the lower-cardinality column always improves compression
mcqs.explanation: Leading with the more selective column (tenant_id, narrowing to one tenant) minimizes the tree slice before the next filter applies, unlike leading with status which only narrows to a fifth of the whole table across every tenant. Order does matter here, and there's no alphabetical rule or universal compression benefit to leading with lower cardinality.

mcqs.question: A query is slow. What should you check before adding a new index to fix it?
options: Nothing — adding an index on the WHERE clause columns is always a safe first move
Whether increasing the server's RAM would be simpler
The `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` plan — to see if an index is missing, being ignored due to a function wrapper or stale statistics, or wouldn't help given the query's actual selectivity
Whether the table needs to be dropped and recreated
mcqs.explanation: The plan reveals the actual cause — missing index, a disabled existing index, bad statistics, or genuinely low selectivity where no index would help — so the fix matches the real problem instead of guessing. Blindly adding an index isn't safe (it's a permanent write cost), and RAM or recreating the table don't address indexing issues directly.
